title: Don't ruin my world (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 7:13)
hook: God shows Adam the trees: all this is for you; don't spoil My world
tomorrow: which verse holds the whole Torah? two rabbis split.

segments.voice: Yesterday: even the urge is good, the drive that builds houses. Today, the same drive near a garden, and the one sentence that keeps it in check.

Somebody hands you the keys to a place: a borrowed car, a friend's apartment for the weekend, a dorm room someone else lived in first. There's always one sentence on the way out the door. Leave it the way you found it. The rabbis imagined God saying a version of that sentence to the first human, in the garden, right after handing him the keys.
screen: `SOMEBODY HANDS YOU THE KEYS.` → `LEAVE IT HOW YOU FOUND IT.` → `THE FIRST SET OF KEYS.`

segments.voice: It's in Ecclesiastes Rabbah, on a verse that sounds tired: "Consider the work of God; for who can make that straight, which He hath made crooked?" When the Holy One created the first human, the midrash says, He took him around all the trees of the garden of Eden and said: see My works, how beautiful and fine they are. Everything I created, I created for you. Take care not to spoil or destroy My world, because if you spoil it, there is no one to repair it after you. Two things live in that speech. The first is gift. The midrash doesn't open with a warning. It opens with a tour, the way you'd walk someone through a house you built for them: this is for you. The second is weight. In the story there's no second gardener coming. Genesis already gives the job, placing the man in the garden "to dress it and to keep it": work it, and guard it. So in this reading, caring for the world isn't a hobby added later. It's there from the start, given in a garden with the trees standing right there. And it's personal. Not the world. My world, and for you.
screen: `A TOUR OF THE TREES.` · `ALL THIS IS FOR YOU.` · `NO ONE TO REPAIR IT AFTER.` · `TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.` · then, large: `DON'T RUIN MY WORLD.`

segments.voice: Find one living thing you can see from where you are: a houseplant, a tree through the window, grass, even a weed in a crack. Look at it for the whole sit, as if someone had just walked you over and said: this is for you. Notice one thing it needs that you could give it this week.
Don't ruin my world: God's words to the first human in Ecclesiastes Rabbah, after a tour of the trees. If it's spoiled, no one comes after to fix it.
Your line: don't ruin my world. It was handed over as a gift. Day fifteen seventy-three.

howItsDone: This midrash is often quoted in Jewish teaching about caring for the environment, including around Tu BiShvat, the new year of the trees, alongside the law of bal tashchit, not wasting or destroying.

chat.meaning: The midrash: all this is for you, so don't ruin My world. Caring for the small piece in front of you is the job.
